name: Runner
subtitle: Continuously moving forward while managing path, obstacles, and rhythm; core is readability and choice cost.
demoRuleHint: Rule: Auto-forward (base 5 m/s) → Obstacle/branch appears → Input (slide/jump/turn) → Judgment (pass/fail) → Speed/combo changes
problemsSolved: Use minimal input to create multiple branching choices (lane/jump/turn/branch).
Standardize obstacle readability and advance notice, reducing "can't see, then die".
Use speed and segment structure to create rhythmic peaks and troughs, avoiding monotonous straight lines.
learningGoals: Beginner: understand the minimal loop — auto-forward → obstacle appears → input → judge → speed change — and reproduce a lane-switch dodge in the demo
Intermediate: write the obstacle-readability contract (lead time, lane spacing, segment rhythm) and shape difficulty with initial speed plus acceleration curve
Advanced: design segment structure with peaks and valleys (difficulty breathing) and verify level pacing with misread rate, survival curve, and per-segment pass rate
minimalRules: Forward speed: base 5 m/s, combo bonus +0.5 m/s per combo, max 8 m/s.

Obstacle judgement: jump pass requires triggering jump within 0.3 s before obstacle, jump height ≥1.2 m; slide pass requires sliding within 0.2 s before obstacle; turn pass requires completing turn when lane spacing ≥1.5 m.
Reward system: collecting items increases combo +1; combo ≥5 triggers combo bonus 1.2× speed; combo lasts 10 s.
systemLoopHint: Input (jump/slide/turn) → Judgment (pass?) → Feedback (speed/combo) → Scene progression → New obstacle → New input

combos.effect: Earn 1 experience point every 10 m; upon reaching 5 points, unlock a new running stance or item, raising the maximum combo cap.
Collect energy items to trigger abilities (e.g., sprint, shield); ability charge accumulates from combos, and combos reset after use.
Procedurally stitch track segments; obstacle types and density are randomly generated along a difficulty curve, maintaining player adaptability.

advancedWarnings: Insufficient readability leads to "reaction failure" rather than "decision failure", causing players to lose rhythm.
Too high obstacle density overwhelms choices, turning the game into pure reaction and reducing depth.
Too low obstacle advance time can actually increase rhythm, but also raises misjudgement rates because players must decide faster, leading to over-anticipation and delayed reaction.
advancedAlgoRefs: Level: segment stitching, difficulty rhythm arrangement.
Judgement: terrain collision, jump trajectory, camera follow.

demoLab.title: Initial Speed Experiment
demoLab.observe: Speed compresses the decision window: at 320px/s the same obstacle lead time halves your reaction budget. Speed doesn’t change obstacle density — it changes the evaluation cost per obstacle. That is the boundary between "died because I couldn’t see" and "died because I couldn’t choose in time"

demoLab.title: Acceleration Curve Contrast
demoLab.action: Run "Acceleration Curve" at 0 and at 30px/s², 60 seconds each
demoLab.observe: At 0 the difficulty is flat and players hit the ceiling fast; at 30px/s² every minute is a new game. An acceleration curve is free difficulty progression at the cost of a slow start — it moves "pacing structure" from level design into parameter design

intro.what: Your character runs forward automatically while you dodge, jump, and slide — Temple Run and Subway Surfers are built on this.
intro.feel: The screen scrolls nonstop as you switch lanes and jump at the last moment; the speed keeps climbing and your palms start sweating — every second asks "how much longer can you last?"
intro.why: It makes "difficulty ramping" tangible — if you want to learn how to raise tension without scaring off beginners, the runner is the standard answer.

concept: Runner play packs difficulty into the time dimension: auto-forward motion turns every second into a decision deadline, so the speed curve IS the difficulty curve. The hard part is not obstacle placement — it is readability engineering: obstacle lead time decides whether a player fails a decision or fails a reaction, and camera plus speed together set the information density. Behind every "this game is fair" review is a precise ratio of lead time to speed.
designNotes: Speed does not change obstacle density — it changes evaluation cost: the same obstacle at 320px/s halves your reaction time. An acceleration curve is free difficulty progression at the price of a tame opening, so the early game must stand on obstacle composition, not speed.

Shorter lead time can improve flow (counterintuitive, but bounded): compressing the warning drops players into pure-instinct flow — past the threshold it degrades into "dead before you see it." Good runners park lead time at the edge of "just barely readable."

Failure must blame the choice, not the reflex: when a player thinks "I didn’t misreact, I picked the wrong lane," they queue another run — engineering "reaction failure" into "decision failure" is the core retention work of runners.
